rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The elution window will guide subsequent window trimming and slope or temperature changes.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the critical first pair responds to slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, preserving the opportunity for a higher score.

The first pair improved only slightly with a shallower gradient, so test temperature selectivity while holding the gradient fixed. Higher temperature should also shorten retention and preserve the zero time penalty.
The maximum CRF is already achieved; shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature at 60 C to retain the favorable selectivity of the first pair.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly relative to injection 4 to recover first-pair resolution while remaining faster than injection 3. The final organic fraction stays comfortably above the observed elution window.
Shift the gradient window upward while preserving the slope of injection 5 to shorten retention. This tests whether the first pair retains baseline resolution with a higher starting organic fraction.

With a maximum-score method secured, test the opposite temperature extreme for a different selectivity that might permit a faster gradient. The broad, eight-minute gradient should elute all compounds without approaching the acquisition limit.

Raise temperature one step to test whether the late three-peak cluster separates while the first pair remains resolved. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates temperature selectivity in this potentially faster operating region.

Return to the favorable 60 C selectivity and use a slope just steeper than injection 5, targeting full resolution in slightly less time. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Test a slightly steeper gradient near the first pair’s resolution boundary to shorten the fully resolved method further. The last peak may enter the final hold, but the endpoint is close to its estimated elution composition, making a long delay unlikely.

Test whether a shallower gradient can compensate for the first-pair resolution lost at a higher starting organic fraction. This probes an alternative maximum-score window while keeping the endpoint above the late-peak elution region.

With several maximum-score methods secured, test whether a much steeper gradient breaks the late-peak coincidence seen at 25 C. This explores a substantially faster method in a distinct selectivity regime.

Probe the resolution boundary between the successful 0.85 endpoint and the slightly under-resolved 0.95 endpoint at ten minutes. This may shorten the last-peak time relative to injection 10 while keeping every pair at R ≥ 1.5.

Test a higher starting composition with a shallower slope to determine whether a narrower window can preserve first-pair resolution. The endpoint remains safely above the late-peak elution region, and maximum-score methods are already secured.

Test whether a higher starting composition and shallower slope separate the late cluster at 30 C while retaining the favorable low-temperature first-pair selectivity. This explores a different window rather than further compressing the nearly limiting 60 C method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 15 to improve the remaining late critical pair and shorten retention. The first pair has some resolution margin, so this may yield another fully resolved operating region.

Make the gradient modestly shallower than injection 16 to bring the first pair above R = 1.5 while retaining resolution of the late pairs. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, potentially securing a maximum-score alternative at moderate temperature.

Return to 60 C and use a slightly shallower slope than injection 3 to increase the limiting first pair’s resolution margin. This should preserve the maximum CRF with the last peak comfortably before 10 minutes.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 11 while retaining its higher starting composition, targeting the first pair’s resolution boundary. This should shorten that maximum-score method while keeping the late peaks inside the gradient.

With the maximum score secured, test a shallower gradient to increase first-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Monitor the third–fourth pair, whose resolution decreases as the gradient becomes shallower.

Refine between injections 11 and 19 with an intermediate slope, targeting full resolution near a seven-minute last-peak time. This should retain slightly more first-pair margin than injection 19 while shortening injection 11.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 20 to shorten retention while preserving useful resolution margins for both early critical pairs. The neighboring slopes tested at 60 C both achieved maximum CRF.

Shorten retention relative to injection 22 with a slope between two successful methods. This targets maximum CRF with more first-pair resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10.

Shorten the programmed gradient from injection 23 while preserving its slope and favorable selectivity. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Use the final injection to test a compact gradient window with a slope between two maximum-score conditions, targeting additional first-pair resolution margin without a time penalty. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
